title: India Just Signed a Trade Deal With Europe. Now It's Begging Brussels Not to Cut Off Its Metal Scrap.
excerpt: The EU's planned scrap export ban could tighten steel and aluminium supply for India's manufacturers — and undermine a trade agreement that isn't even in force yet.
body:
India has formally asked the European Union for an exemption from planned curbs on metal scrap exports, warning that restrictions on a material its steel and aluminium industries depend on could raise costs, tighten supply, and undermine the very trade agreement the two sides just signed.

The request, first reported by Reuters on Monday, comes as the EU prepares to enforce its revised waste shipment regulation from May 2027. Under the new rules, exports of non-hazardous waste — including ferrous and aluminium scrap — to countries outside the OECD will be banned unless the EU grants an explicit exemption by November 2026. India, as a non-OECD economy, is directly in the firing line.

"The EU is a key supplier of high-quality ferrous scrap to India and any export curbs could tighten supply and raise costs for domestic steelmakers," said Pankaj Chadha, chairman of the Engineering Export Promotion Council of India.

The stakes are significant. India, the world's second-largest crude steel producer, imported approximately 366,000 tonnes of aluminium scrap from the EU in 2025 and was the bloc's single largest buyer in the first quarter of 2026. On the European side, aluminium scrap exports reached a record 1.27 million metric tonnes in 2025 — roughly 50 per cent above 2019 levels — with the largest share heading to Asia, and the highest volume to India.

The European Commission is also considering additional, separate measures specifically targeting aluminium scrap exports. Those plans, initially expected by spring 2026, have been pushed back to September amid what industry sources describe as the difficulty of balancing producers who want to keep scrap at home for recycling against recyclers and exporters who profit from selling it abroad. European Aluminium, the lobby group representing continental producers, supports the restrictions. Recycling Europe, whose members include companies that shred cars and extract aluminium, opposes them.

For India, the timing could not be worse. This year's India-EU free trade agreement — the product of years of stop-and-start negotiations — is set to take effect early next year. While the deal covers tariff reductions, market access, and regulatory cooperation across dozens of sectors, it does not provide direct relief from the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which became fully operational this year and hits India's steel and aluminium exporters especially hard.

"India moved from threatening confrontation over the CBAM to negotiating the terms of engagement within it," noted a recent analysis by IANS. "Whether that engagement converts into relief that the Indian industry can actually use remains open — a question the FTA's text alone cannot answer."

Now, on top of the carbon levies, India faces a potential raw material squeeze. The EU's planned scrap ban would effectively remove one of India's cheapest inputs for secondary steel and aluminium production. Industry representatives have raised the issue directly with India's commerce ministry, which has formally applied to Brussels to retain access under the new waste shipment regime. A government official, speaking on condition of anonymity, suggested that export quotas rather than a complete ban could emerge as a compromise.

The scrap issue has also been complicated by a recent decision from the United Arab Emirates to ban scrap exports. India normally sources about 20 per cent of its scrap from Gulf states. With the UAE shutting that door and the EU threatening to follow, Indian recyclers and secondary producers face a narrowing list of reliable suppliers.

"We're naturally impatient due to the scale and urgency of the problems, but this is about the next five years, not the next five weeks," said Paul Voss, director general of European Aluminium, defending the slow pace of the EU's deliberations.

The scrap restriction is part of a broader European push to retain raw materials for its own green transition. Aluminium recycling uses 95 per cent less energy than producing primary metal from mined bauxite, making scrap a cornerstone of the EU's decarbonisation strategy. Brussels argues that exporting scrap undermines its climate goals.

India, however, makes the opposite argument: its manufacturers need imported scrap precisely because domestic collection infrastructure is still developing, and restricting supply would push them toward energy-intensive primary production — worsening emissions, not reducing them.

The disagreement lays bare a tension at the heart of the new India-EU partnership. The trade agreement was sold as a vehicle for deeper economic integration, but the scrap and CBAM disputes show how quickly real-world industrial policy can collide with the cooperative language of trade diplomacy. For India's steelmakers and aluminium smelters, the question is no longer whether Europe is a reliable trade partner, but whether the deal both sides celebrated will survive its first year of implementation.
